newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria Creditanstalt marathon enters new last lap.
newsitem.headline: Austria Creditanstalt marathon enters new last lap.

text.p: A glimmer of a rapprochement between Austria's divided government coalition partners was seen on Friday after the Social Democrats hinted they may seek a compromise in the disputed sale of Creditanstalt.

The privatisation of the country's second biggest bank, now in its seventh year, has caused sharp divisions between the Social Democrats (SPOe) and the conservative People's Party (OeVP), their junior partner, after arch-rival Bank Austria entered the fray for Creditanstalt last month.

Bank Austria, effectively controlled by the SPOe-dominated City of Vienna, is the SPOe's candidate of choice. But this option is strongly disliked by the OeVP, which is closely allied with conservative stronghold Creditanstalt.
Bank Austria is up against a rival bid by an international group led by insurer EA-Generali -- endorsed by the conservatives -- and an outside offer by former Austrian retail tycoon Karl Wlaschek.
According to the SPOe's latest proposal, the state's 70 percent voting stake in Creditanstalt should be sold to the highest bidder, whose shares would then be widely distributed via the bourse.
Bank Austria's bid tops EA-Generali's offer by almost three billion schillings ($275.2 million). No details of Wlaschek's offer, reportedly backed by a large German bank, have been released.
The OeVP, whose vociferous rejection of Bank Austria has raised the spectre of a government collapse, gave a guarded welcome to the Social Democrat's foray.
"I'm satisfied that we have departed from the rigid starting positions," chief whip Andreas Khol told state television.

Social Democrat Finance Minister Viktor Klima originally wanted to wrap up Europe's longest running privatisation by the end of last year, but the troubled government coalition was given some breathing space when he decided on December 30 to allow bidders until January 10 to improve their offers.

While analysts rejected the SPOe proposal as "economically unwise", sources close to the talks said the latest political wrangles in the seemingly endless selloff saga gave no reason to believe a solution of the privatisation muddle was imminent.
The conservatives insist on a special emergency session of parliament to discuss the sale on January 14, four days after the latest -- and supposedly final -- tender closes.

Chief whip Khol indicated his party would not seek a vote of no confidence against Klima should he pick a buyer between those dates, but party leader and Vice Chancellor Wolfgang Schuessel on Friday told Austrian state radio Klima would face at least some "problems in parliament" in that case.
The SPOe insists parliament has no say in the sale of Creditanstalt, which by law is Klima's responsibility.
"Calling for a special session of parliament makes no sense and could harm Austria," SPOe finance spokesman Ewald Nowotny said.
SPOe general secretary Brigitte Ederer called on the OeVP, the Social Democrat's coalition partner for 10 years, to step back from the brink of a looming government collapse.
"All parties, and most of all the OeVP, should calm down a little. We must find the solution that is in the best interest of the tax payer," she said. ($1=10.90 Schilling)
